title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)

icd10.label: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma

definition: Acute metabolic emergency defined by the triad of hyperglycemia, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia, caused by absolute insulin deficiency.
typical_patient: Younger patient with type 1 DM — frequently the first presentation of undiagnosed T1DM. Also occurs in ketosis-prone type 2 DM.
pathophysiology: Absolute insulin deficiency removes the brake on lipolysis. Free fatty acids flood the liver and are converted to ketoacids (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) faster than they can be buffered. Counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines) simultaneously drive gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Result: hyperglycemia plus a true anion-gap acidosis. Osmotic diuresis from glucosuria then produces profound volume and potassium depletion — total body potassium is low even when serum potassium reads normal or high.
precipitants: Infection — the single most common trigger
SGLT2 inhibitors — can cause euglycemic DKA with near-normal glucose

key_findings.label: Glucose
key_findings.value: Typically 250–600 mg/dL. May be under 250 in euglycemic DKA.

key_findings.label: Ketones
key_findings.value: Positive — beta-hydroxybutyrate preferred over urine ketones

symptoms: Kussmaul respirations — deep and labored, blowing off CO2
Dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension

plan_bullets.text: Admit for inpatient management; ICU-level care for pH under 7.0, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability.
Begin isotonic 0.9% NaCl 15–20 mL/kg IV over the first hour. Estimated deficit 3–6 L.
After the first hour, transition to 0.45% NaCl if corrected sodium is normal or elevated; continue 0.9% NaCl if corrected sodium is low.
Check serum potassium BEFORE starting insulin. If K under 3.3 mEq/L, hold insulin and replete potassium first.
If K is 3.3–5.2 mEq/L, add 20–30 mEq potassium per liter of IV fluid to maintain K at 4–5.
Start regular insulin IV infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr. Target a glucose decline of 50–75 mg/dL/hr.
When glucose reaches 200 mg/dL, add dextrose (D5) to IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion until the anion gap closes.
Overlap subcutaneous basal insulin with the IV infusion by 1–2 hours before discontinuing the drip.
BMP and glucose every 2–4 hours until the anion gap closes and the patient is clinically stable.
Identify the precipitant: CBC with differential, urinalysis and culture, chest radiograph, ECG, and troponin as indicated.

medications.note: IV route only in acute DKA. Never start before potassium is known.
Fluids come first — they lower glucose before insulin does.

medications.dose: 20–30 mEq/L of IV fluid when K is 3.3–5.2
medications.note: Insulin drives K intracellularly. Unreplaced, this causes fatal arrhythmia.
Routine use is not supported and may worsen outcomes.

pearls: Fluids before insulin, and potassium before insulin. Insulin given to a hypokalemic patient can kill them.
Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3). Normal is 8–12.
Corrected sodium = measured Na + 1.6 for every 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100.
Do not stop the insulin drip when glucose normalizes — stop it when the GAP closes. Add dextrose instead.
Euglycemic DKA: a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor can be frankly acidotic with a glucose of 180. Check ketones and the gap on any SGLT2 patient with nausea and vomiting.
Roughly a third of patients present with overlapping DKA and HHS features. It is a spectrum, not two boxes.
when_to_refer: All confirmed DKA — emergency department, then inpatient. This is not managed outpatient.
ICU admission for pH under 7.0, bicarbonate under 5, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability.
Pediatric DKA — escalate early; children are at risk for cerebral edema during correction.
New-onset type 1 diabetes — endocrinology consult before discharge.
patient_education: Sick day rule: never stop your insulin when you are ill, even if you are not eating. Illness raises your insulin needs, it does not lower them.
Check your blood glucose every 4 hours while sick.
Check ketones any time your glucose is over 250 mg/dL, or any time you have nausea and vomiting.
Drink sugar-free fluids steadily to stay ahead of dehydration.
Call immediately for moderate or large ketones, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, glucose over 300 that will not come down, or trouble breathing.
resolution_criteria: Glucose under 200 mg/dL, AND two of the following:
Calculated anion gap 12 mEq/L or less
